Lesotho -South Africa porous borders

By: Sinethemba Nogude | Commission

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
This story investigates the growing crisis of illegal border crossings between Lesotho and South Africa. Through compelling accounts from affected farmers, victims of vehicle theft, and overwhelmed law enforcement, it highlights the human and economic cost of unchecked crime and border insecurity.
We will also have access to transporters who help illegal crossers into South Africa. We will be able to show how lax border control is at the Tele and Qacha Nek crossing in the Eastern Cape.
We will also have access to chiefs who have been struggling to clamp down on illegal immigrants crossing into their villages and have set up camp and assumed citizenship.

Summary:
Summary:
South Africa’s border with Lesotho is at the center of a troubling crime wave. Every week, stolen vehicles are smuggled across the Caledon River, livestock vanish in the night, and communities face violence from armed gangs. A recent incident in the Eastern Cape saw unclaimed corpses of illegal crossers underscore the deadly risks of these journeys. Despite efforts by SANDF and police, resource constraints leave the border largely open to exploitation.

Further information:
This episode will explore:

The tactics used by criminals to smuggle cars and livestock.
Firsthand accounts from farmers whose livelihoods are threatened daily.
The risks illegal migrants face crossing the river and the desperation that drives them.
Law enforcement and military efforts to control the chaos and their limitations.
Approach:
Field Interviews and Scenes:

Interviews with affected farmers in the Free State and Eastern Cape.
SAPS officials stationed at the border.
Voices of local community leaders grappling with rising crime.
:
Statistics from border patrol operations.
Drone footage capturing border vulnerabilities.
Broader Impact:

The economic toll on agriculture and communities.
Insights from migration and crime experts on cross-border criminal syndicates.

Script:


LESOTHO BORDER
V/O
In these hills, the name Ntsane Motlokoa - a community leader and skilled tracker - is well known.

Last year, he set off on the trail of livestock stolen from a local farmer, a regular service he provided here in the foothills of the Maluti Mountains in the Eastern Free State.

But, in the darkness of an August night, a fatal encounter changed everything…




Bam!
V/O
Clarens in the Eastern Free State. Famous for its cafés, galleries and mountain views, it’s just a short drive from our border with Lesotho.


V/O
It’s a popular getaway for local visitors, but in recent years the people living here have found little peace.
Upsound Duncan Martin Interview in the fieldFX3 6707T01
In this valley alone there used to be over 12 farmers 10 years ago. There are four of us left now doing full-time farming.
V/O
Duncan Martin is a local livestock farmer. After more than two decades here, he - like many others - lives and works under siege.
Upsound Duncan Martin interview in the fieldsFX3 6707T01
Masa: 01:10 Tell me about the problems you're facing…?

Duncan: 01:38 *sigh* Our stock tends to get stolen on a regular basis. where a gang or a group of men will come in here for two weeks and they will literally target just about every single person who owns cattle in the entire valley.


V/O
The more than 900 km border with Lesotho winds through a rugged and largely unmonitored landscape… perfect terrain for criminals. With few physical barriers and limited patrols, syndicates are able to move anything from drugs to stolen vehicles and even livestock across the border.
Upsound Duncan Martin interview in the fields FX3 6707T01
04:42 The cattle get stolen and they might use the border of Lesotho as a way to get ahead of us Because they know we can't just cross into Lesotho

Upsound Masa FX3 6707T01 03:01Is there no fence, no border patrol or anything between this side and Lesotho?

Upsound Duncan Martin Interview in the fields03:01 FX3 6707T01 : Geographically, we don't have a border fence. We've got a small river, the Caledon, Tthey can just hop over the mountain.
V/O
The Defence Force is responsible for securing our borders. But, with violent crime surging, not only are they failing, says Duncan, the problem is getting worse.
Upsound Duncan Martin Interview in the fields FX3 6707T01 02:06
02:06 About 10 years ago, it started becoming a problem. Where they would come and steal 10, 20, 30 cows in a night, 200 sheep.

Upsound Duncan Martin interview in the fields FX3 6707T01 02:33 And in the last 3-5 years, the big problem has become that the thieves have become more and more aggressive, armed and dangerous.


Upsound Duncan Martin Interview in the fields FX3 6707T01 20:51
When we approached with our vehicle in the night in the mountain we didn’t realise where these guys were and they opened fire on us. And fortunately their aim was bad…
V/O
Others, like Ntsane Motlokoa, weren’t as lucky.


[breather/transition ]
Upsound Keletso Motlokoa
03:30 He liked to communicate, he liked to laugh, he liked to make jokes. Yeah, he was a good man, a very good man. What do you miss most about him in the house? Oh, laughing. Laughing a lot. You know, he used to say, I cannot go on a vacation without my family. So he made sure, he always made sure that he's around his family. Yeah, I miss, he's laughing a lot.


V/O
His son, Keletso, recalls his father setting off towards the mountains to track and recover stolen cattle. He says it was a clear August day.


Upsound Keletso Motlokoa
04:46 He was going to join a police officer and other three shepherds from that farm where the cows were stolen.
V/O
When he couldn’t get hold of his father, Keletso grew worried.
Upsound Keletso Motlokoa


Upsound Keletso Motlokoa
06:00At 1, 2 out of luck, I tried to call him. I don't know why, but I tried to call him. And he's not picking up his phone. , the phone is not ringing. I'm like, no, this is unlike my father.


V/O
Eventually, he was able to reach the police officer who left with his father earlier that day.
Upsound Keletso Motlokoa


… but your father was shot…
Upsound Duncan Martin Interview in the fields FX3 6707T01
16:22 And that was a breaking point for all of us. It was one thing to be losing hundreds of thousands of rands of stock and valuables, of having your property continuously trespassed upon. That's one thing. But when an important and a very good person from your community has to be murdered in cold blood, that's where we drew the line.


V/O
Outraged by Ntsane Motlokoa’s death, Duncan and other farmers, landowners, and residents drew a line in the sand,.......turning to a specialised anti-poaching unit to patrol the lawless frontier.




[ pause]
V/O
Early on a Tuesday night, we join Duncan on patrol with the security team.


Duncan Martin
Duncan Upsound FX3 6792 07:00 We're going to meet them at their base at this point. Mm-hmm. And they are going to deploy, fortunately for them, some of them deploy on foot now and they'll be heading into the mountain to a specific point


V/O
They’re highly trained and well-armed.


Upsound Masa and Duncan FX3 6808 :01:56 What kinds of things, I mean of course they are equipped and they are armed and they are skilled, but [ Masa] What kinds of dangers could they and do they possibly run into here? Like we spoke earlier,[Duncan] ]they could come across a gang of six to twelve guys out there, all armed, all ready for a fight. There are various things, they might even come across
Upsound Duncan FX3 6808 02:27 Also marijuana smugglers, who will also come with armed people who would be there to protect them. They don't know what they will meet out there. They don't know who they will meet out




[ a bit of patrolling tense shots]


Masa Link FX3 6830 :
I can't help but wonder how they make their way through this terrain and just how dark it is, lets turn off the lights so that you can have a clear picture


V/O
It’s ideal cover for criminals and the team is on edge.
Masa Link FX3 6811
Unfortunately this is as far as we can go on this night patrol, the guys are going to go and do their thing because it's too dangerous… [ there might be a better version]




Upsound Jacques Smith FX3 6997 day 4
11:19 You see the overgrazing? I mean there's nothing left here. Look at all the fences.
V/O


Lesotho is experiencing a crippling drought, and many of its livestock farmers are also exploiting the porous border. They cross illegally with their herds, grazing on both communal and private farmland— causing significant damage. It’s a serious problem in Wepener, right on the border with Lesotho.
Upsound Jacques Smith FX3 6997
2:46 Hundreds and hundreds of cattle coming over every single night into Wepener.
[Masa] But why do they need to graze here? Why don't they graze in Lesotho?
[Jacque]There's no more grass in Lesotho. It's so overgrazed.



V/O
This farmer asked us to hide his identity for safety reasons.


Upsound Jacques Smith FX3 6997 day 4 17:22 Every single winter, they burn the form to the ground. The Lesotho, because they want the green grass to come out. They burn that farm to the rocks.
V/O
This region is ideal for cattle and sheep ranching, and staple crops like wheat and maize… but farmers are backed into a corner. With land values collapsing, their futures are on the line.
Upsound Jacques Smith FX3 6997
4:59 just because of the border.15:26
market value has fallen so much that you can't even buy it. You can't even sell it for, I mean there’s border ground that’s going for just over R1000 per hectare.


V/O
Relentless livestock theft is a problem here, too - something we experience first hand. Midway through our interview, the farmer gets an alarming call..


Upsound Jacques Smith FX3 6997
18:00 Tell me about where we're going now. Sorry. I've just received a call for the fence that's been cut. And there's wool in the fence. And this is one of the main routes when they steal sheep as they come through.


V/O
When we arrive, it's already too late—his sheep are gone.
Upsound Jacques Smith
00:04 [Masa] So what are we looking for?[Jacques] Well, first of all, we want to see if there's any livestock gone through the fence where it's cut. Is that the fence? Yeah, this is where it's cut. Oh, it is cut. There you can see there's a sheep's spoor. There's a fresh track of sheep. Oh, I see.

Upsound Jacques Smith FX3 7006 00:50 Masa I mean, how does that make you feel, ? I mean, that's your sheep there, gone, just like that. Well, it makes you agitated, because, I mean, you've got not just the financial impact. It's all the work now. I just want to farm. . But you're so busy keeping everything off your shoulders and the crisis control that you never get to farm.






V/O
At the border between the two countries, we discover for ourselves the chaos we’ve been hearing about.
Upsound Jacques Smith
01:56 [Masa] So this is it, huh?[Jacques] This is the border. You must use your imagination. Yeah, because I can't see it. Yeah, but this is the border. This? This. It's a joke. So I'm in Lesotho, and you're in South Africa. And if I go like, I mean, I just don't want to commit a crime. But if I do that with my foot and I step this side, I'm in Lesotho illegally. And what's stopping me from doing this? This pole.



V/O
Km upon km are unfenced, the roads crumbling and only occasional signs of what was once a secure boundary.


Upsound Jacques Smith 14:03 [ Masa] And at this border, typically what makes it a cross? { Jacques Anything. Illegal immigrants, drugs, thieves.

Upsound Jacques Smith border 04:51[ Masa ] It's almost like you've been left to your own devices. Yeah. I would like to know when last the local police has been here.


V/O
And here too, the criminals are brazen.
Upsound Jacque at border
Upsound Jaqcues at Border13:10 Sometimes they even recognize me and they say, hey, Retlo Bulaya That means we're gonna kill you.


[pause]
Upsound Masa at the border walk and talk
00:02:48 : We are in Telle in the Eastern Cape, we are meeting a couple of guys who work as guides and assistants for people who are crossing the border illegally.


V/O
In January, our producer went undercover here at Telle, one of the busiest entry points to the Eastern Cape.

So-called “transporters" openly operate, offering to smuggle him into Lesotho. No documents needed, no patrols in sight.
UPS
Laughing
V/O

The transporters offered a return trip too, this time via the official border post: no passports stamped, no names recorded.

Casually slipping through unnoticed by South Africa’s Border Management Agency.

(PAUSE)

I arranged to meet them on THIS visit, too.
V/O
Called “Dikepe” or “Boats”, they know the area well. For as little R150, they provide round-trip travel to and from South Africa. They insisted we hide their identities.


Upsound TRANSPORTER 1
00:06:57 If you want to know everything, He is Sotho, and those people are coming from South Africa going to Lesotho.
Upsound Masa
00:06:59: Which people?
Upsound 00:07:05 TRANSPORTER1:
00:07:05 : They don’t have passports, so they are crossing over the river then go to the taxi rank.
Upsound Masa
00:25:58 It is said that there are some people that transport cars, weed, drugs, guns illegally. Are there people who do that?


Upsound TRANSPORTER1
00:26:09 : There are some other people that carry guns, others drugs but they don’t go where there are police,.
V/O
Many of the illegal crossings here are driven by Lesotho’s deep economic challenges. It’s a situation aggravated by low police and military visibility and what people here told us is a culture of accepting bribes.
Upsound Masa
00:38:32 : Were you not afraid that the cops can come up to you and ask you for your particulars?
Upsound illegal border Lady 1
00:38:38 I was afraid because I do not have them.
Upsound Masa :
Upsound 00:38:41 : What gave you courage that even when you are that scared you still went?


Upsound illegal border Lady 1
00:38:47: Circumstances, knowing that my kids don’t have food or means to go to school, such things.
Upsound illegal border Lady 1
Upsound 00:38:56 Lady 1: Even now I left them crying, I was crying too but I had to leave.
Upsound illegal border Lady 1
00:38:59 : [ woman breaks down]
Upsound Masa
38:59 : It will all be ok, you will be ok, you will find a job, your kids will be ok, you will go back home having fixed your things to travel legally.


V/O
Later, we encounter trauma of a different kind. In this lawless frontier, no one is safe.
Upsound illegal border Lady 2 Masa
00:46:31 : What happened, ma?


Upsound illegal border Lady 2
00:46:35 : I am in need of transportation, I don’t have transport to get to where I am going right now.
V/O
This woman and her partner were robbed while crossing the border illegally.
Upsound illegal border Lady 2
00:47:06 : These people asked us to give them R450 and we told them that we don’t have it.
Upsound illegal border Lady 2
00:47:18 Lady: When we got here we told them that we don’t have it and they searched him and took all the money he had.
Upsound illegal border Lady 2 Masa
00:47:22 Interviewer: All of it?, and it’s the money you were supposed to pay for you transportation with?
Upsound illegal border Lady 2
00:47:25 Lady: Yes we were going to use it for transport.




Upsound FX3_6504 day 2 Masa
00:03:41 Masa: How many people cross here in a day?
Upsound transporter FX3_6504 day 2
00:03:45 Interviewee: I am not sure, maybe 150 to 400 or 500 a day.
Upsound Masa FX3_6504 day 2
00:03:49 : A day?
Upsound transporter FX3_6504 day 2
00:03:53 : yes, in 1 day.
V/O
And it’s getting worse—even those with valid documents are now bypassing the border post and crossing illegally – it’s simply far less hassle.
Upsound transporter FX3_6504 day 2
00:04:09 : Yes, there are there, that have valid passports some of them they don’t have them, some are scared that they will be given few days.
00:04:18 : At the end their passport will be fined, that’s why people prefer coming this side and most of the people are people with passport.
V/ O
This border is more than a line dividing two countries, it’s a trade and smuggling route to many, a lifeline to others. It’s a crisis of weak enforcement where criminality thrives. And, as hope of a solution fades, communities along this chaotic frontier wonder for how much longer they’ll be able to hold out.
[end]

metadata.Unique Selling Point: This story investigates the growing crisis of illegal border crossings between Lesotho and South Africa. Through compelling accounts from affected farmers, victims of vehicle theft, and overwhelmed law enforcement, it highlights the human and economic cost of unchecked crime and border insecurity. We will also have access to transporters who help illegal crossers into South Africa. We will be able to show how lax border control is at the Tele and Qacha Nek crossing in the Eastern Cape. We will also have access to chiefs who have been struggling to clamp down on illegal immigrants crossing into their villages and have set up camp and assumed citizenship.
metadata.Summary: Summary: South Africa’s border with Lesotho is at the center of a troubling crime wave. Every week, stolen vehicles are smuggled across the Caledon River, livestock vanish in the night, and communities face violence from armed gangs. A recent incident in the Eastern Cape saw unclaimed corpses of illegal crossers underscore the deadly risks of these journeys. Despite efforts by SANDF and police, resource constraints leave the border largely open to exploitation.
metadata.Further information: This episode will explore: The tactics used by criminals to smuggle cars and livestock. Firsthand accounts from farmers whose livelihoods are threatened daily. The risks illegal migrants face crossing the river and the desperation that drives them. Law enforcement and military efforts to control the chaos and their limitations. Approach: Field Interviews and Scenes: Interviews with affected farmers in the Free State and Eastern Cape. SAPS officials stationed at the border. Voices of local community leaders grappling with rising crime. : Statistics from border patrol operations. Drone footage capturing border vulnerabilities. Broader Impact: The economic toll on agriculture and communities. Insights from migration and crime experts on cross-border criminal syndicates.
